238.t: The Dunbar Hotel lounge and the plan to restore it
238.s: She confirms she worked in the Dunbar lounge and gives her doubts about restoring the hotel because the neighborhood has changed.
238.q: Just the Dunbar Lounge, Dunbar Hotel Lounge. Incidentally, this is the lounge that you have been reading about in the paper -- the hotel, rather, that they are trying to restore.

238.t: Dunbar and Clarke hotels and the old Local 767
238.s: She and Willard work out the Dunbar's origins and the Clarke Hotel, near Local 767, the black musicians' local used for rehearsals before amalgamation.
238.q: I don't really know, but I did know the Clarke Hotel was -- I think the Dunbar was before the Clarke. I think so. I'm not sure. Because it was in a different area, you know.

238.t: Paul Howard recruits her into the union
238.s: Paul Howard persuaded her to join with a $25 fee paid in installments; her pay rose from $2 to $3 a night.
238.q: Well, he was. Oh, he certainly was. He was a dear -- he's a dear man, and thank God he's still around. Paul Howard was -- well, he was a very union minded person, you know, and of course as I say, I was here about two years before I joined the union. Well, you didn't really have to join the union.…

238.t: What the trial board and Board of Directors do
238.s: She explains the trial board hears claims, the Board of Directors makes policy and hears appeals, and the International Executive Board is the final appeal.
238.q: Well, the trial board, you make decisions on cases, you know. You process cases and claims. If a member has been done in, we'll say. Maybe he has a claim or somebody owes him money, whether it's a proprietor or whatever, a record company or whatever, and he hasn't been able to get this money, well,…

238.t: Elmer Fain, bandleader turned union agent
238.s: Saxophonist Elmer Fain led a band before becoming business agent of Local 767 and later 47.
238.ch: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
238.q: Yes, indeed, and it's been like that through the years. Well, he was here when I first came here, and guys like -- well, Elmer Fain, who we mentioned earlier. Elmer Fain has been around Los Angeles -- he was here when I first came here, and later I think Elmer Fain might have had an orchestra at…

238.t: Union benefits, scale and refusing low pay
238.s: Early benefits were a $250 death payment; scale meant turning down work, but as membership grew musicians gained bargaining power.
238.q: Well, I think, if I'm not mistaken, I think you only go -- I think it was $250.00. That was, you know, your death benefit. That's what you got out of it, $250.00. And of course the dues, I don't remember what the dues were at that time, but it wasn't very much, you know. And this is -- you know,…

238.t: Joining in 1937 and the amalgamation of Local 767 into 47
238.s: She joined around 1937; on amalgamation in the 1950s members kept seniority, received a $1,000 death benefit and the old assets passed to 47.
238.q: And the one nice thing, the one thing I have to say, the benefit, when the union finally -- when the unions, rather, when they amalgamated, part of the bargain was for us to maintain our -- I was going to say seniority, we'll

238.t: Opposition to amalgamation and working mostly in white clubs
238.s: Some older members opposed merging, and she says she always worked in white establishments rather than black spots.
238.q: Of course they had some opposition, from what they tell me. In fact I think some of the older members that are still around, they naturally did not see the advantage, you know. They were so used to going down to the old union. But the wonderful force behind the whole thing really won over, and it…

238.t: Her seat on the Board of Local 47
238.s: Harvey Brooks's death opened a trial board seat for her; Marl Young and John Tranchitella urged her to serve, and she is now on her third term on the Board.
238.q: Well, Harvey Brooks was a dear friend. He was a wonderful man, a wonderful friend and a very talented man with many, many wonderful tunes to his credit. He was a great ASCAP man, also. He was one of the guys who encouraged me to get into ASCAP, you know. In fact my publisher was the first one to…

238.t: Union benefits and the officers of the old local
238.s: Howard explained life membership and protection of pay; she names officers including Florence Cadrez, Ed Bailey and Leo Davis.
238.q: of this, you know, he explained all of this to you, and he would take the time and go on to explain to you the advantages of being in the union. He says, 'Now, when you work you have a chance of making more money.' And he says, 'Not only that, if you don't get your money the union can protect you.…

238.t: Paul Howard, the early Local 767 and its building on Central Avenue
238.s: The early black local was nearly nothing until Paul Howard's membership drive and the purchase of an old house on Central Avenue.
238.q: you know -- there was a union. I don't even remember where it was located, but there was a union on Vernon or someplace, but it was nothing.

29.t: How the union started and Howard became financial secretary
29.s: Howard says the early bands were nonunion, that he had nothing to do with forming Local 767, and that he took his outside experience inside the union.
29.ch: The union and the 1920s-30s band scene
29.q: Yeah, it was nonunion. But they soon got that straightened out. It didn't take long, because we were always pushing to do the right thing. And that was the right thing, to have a union band.

29.t: Who led Local 767: Press Johnson, Robinson and Marshall Royal's father
29.s: Collette and Howard try to recall the union's early presidents; Press Johnson, a businessman named Robinson and Marshall Royal's father (secretary) come up.
29.ch: The union and the 1920s-30s band scene
29.q: And did you know -- there's one other person I want to know did you know real well. But he's not -- his name doesn't come to me right now, but it will in a few minutes. Now, if we'll shut this machine off for a minute, --

29.t: Mixed bands and the merging of the black and white unions
29.s: Willard and Collette discuss segregated bands at the Cotton Club and the post-war push to merge the two unions, with Howard commenting.
29.ch: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
29.q: That they didn't want to do and things like that.

29.t: Howard as a mentor to young musicians and the initiation fee break
29.s: Collette says Howard inspired Hamilton, Mingus, Dolphy and others, and arranged a two-week reduced initiation fee for nonunion players.
29.ch: Union career, Masons, mentoring and the Clef Club

29.t: A 1934 news story of musicians suing a dance promoter
29.s: Willard and Collette read a Hollywood Filmograph story about Elmer Fain's band suing for pay with the union head Mr. Johnson; Howard knows nothing of it.
29.ch: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
29.q: Let's see, this paper was -- this was a '34 issue.

29.t: Schooling and becoming a Past Master Mason
29.s: Howard says the union job pushed him to study, which led to becoming a Past Master of his Masonic lodge.
29.ch: Union career, Masons, mentoring and the Clef Club
29.q: Oh, boy, she played the devil out of a piano. Make you sick with a piano. And then when I got working for the union, when I got that job up there at the union, and they told me I had to go to school. And I went to school and studied. But I didn't think it was going to be that long. I didn't think…

29.s: Howard says he started the Clef Club as a monthly chartered social club with no playing, apart from the union.
29.ch: Union career, Masons, mentoring and the Clef Club
29.q: One of the main men we had to get out of it was Arthur Twine. We couldn't keep him in,

29.s: Howard and Collette run through who belongs, including Buddy Banks, Alton Redd and Ted Brinson.
29.ch: Union career, Masons, mentoring and the Clef Club
29.q: That's all, see because a lot of those members, a lot of those fellows, will never be nothing but what they are now.

29.t: The Masonic requirement of the Clef Club
29.s: Howard says members must be Masons and musicians, and asks that his role in founding it not be recorded.
29.ch: Union career, Masons, mentoring and the Clef Club
29.q: That's a little different. Just a little difference. I've got the list of the members here, and I wish I could get it back here and let you see it, who's in the club and all like that, but I don't -- I can't tell you just what they're doing, you know.

29.t: Cleaning at the union and rising to financial secretary
29.s: After leaving playing he took a union cleaning job, later became financial secretary, and went to school for accounting.
29.ch: Union career, Masons, mentoring and the Clef Club
29.q: I took a job up there and I was -- at the union, cleaning up the place, you know, like that. And I didn't have to do it.

232.t: Attending the national union convention and the union's weakness
232.s: He meets Gibbens at union conventions and thinks the union is getting weak and says he pushed a by-law.
232.ch: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
232.q: been going to the national convention--and I got acquainted with Basie and he brought back remembrances and this and that and so on and we've been very close the last few years and since we're speaking about the union, he and discussed how it is, and frankly speaking, I think it's getting weak. You…

232.t: Tony Twist's lawsuit against Zigfields and the Local 94 by-law
232.s: After Local 94 had to fight Zigfields in court, Fields wins a by-law for civil suits at the local's expense.
232.ch: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
232.q: for you. So finally a new club, two or three years ago, opened up in Tulsa, Zigfields, and a boy got a gig in there, a nice paying gig, right locally, which you know yourself, about twenty five hundred a week right there on location, and they had some kind of trouble with the crowd and he fired him…

232.t: Joining Dallas Local 168 and founding Tulsa's Black Local 808
232.s: Black musicians could not join the white Tulsa local, so Fields joined Dallas 168, then helped found Local 808, later merged into 94.
232.ch: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
232.q: I could remember about the union, as I said, how come unions--you see, unions used to be strong you might say in the twenties and thirties, and especially for the blacks, because so many didn't belong, and when I began to play around and attract a little attention, well, I'd send somebody for work…

232.t: Going as a delegate to the Hawaii convention
232.s: Substituting for an ill vice president, he is shown a resolution requiring merged locals to send a Black delegate.
232.ch: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
232.q: One year the vice president of our local, they had president, vice president and treasurer, by the by-laws, three would go. And so, this vice had open heart surgery and couldn't go, so they sent me in his place, and I'll never forget, we were in Hawaii and I was tickled to death to get that ride to…

232.t: Lining up speakers and the secretary's objection
232.s: Fields talks to speakers before the session; his own secretary worries the resolution will invite other groups' demands.
232.ch: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
232.q: So that was in there, and so I said I'm glad you join that attention and he said the only thing about it, it never had come up and he said today is the last day, this was early in the morning, he said we've got to see--we were just waiting around before the meeting was over--during the meeting…

232.t: Speaking at mike seven and passing the resolution
232.s: He speaks for the Black delegate resolution and the hall stands unanimously, except one man from Florida.
232.ch: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
232.q: So anyway, when that went to come up I got up, I was near mike seven, when I got up the secretary and president almost turned white, they wondered what I was going to say. So many were jumping for it, white and black, and so I got to standing there so long, one guy next to me was going around and I…

232.t: Weak unions in small towns, and Marvin Young the lawyer and arranger
232.s: Love and Fields agree unions are weak outside the big cities; Fields tells how he gave Marvin Young an arrangement and Young became a fine arranger.
232.ch: Local 94, Local 808 and the union convention
232.q: Definitely so, and really, believe it or not Preston, it's a little weak, I think, even in the larger towns. We have a black secretary out there, Marvin Young,--

232.t: Ernie Jr.'s dispute with Bobby Bland's management
232.s: Junior led Bobby Bland's band, sued over unpaid money and hit union and management complications; Fields wishes he had taught him the union ways.
232.q: One thing you talk about the union, that is where (inaudible), that's one time I wish I trained Ernie, Jr. along those lines.

232.t: Working with the Mills Brothers and the Coquille, Oregon story
232.s: He backed the Mills Brothers in the East and in Oregon, where the Mills Brothers' mocking autograph jokes recall a Tulsa union dispute.
232.q: I'll tell you a coincidence with the Mills Brothers; I worked with them several times so when I was on the west coast there I turned short a lot--I mean to be frank, I didn't have as big a class music like I had a lot of times, but I was satisfying Mr. Public.

98.t: Two segregated locals with different scales; the Josephine Baker bind
98.s: Black Local 208 and white Local 10 had different scales; hiring Local 10 accordion and violin players for Josephine Baker at the Regal brought Saunders trouble.
98.q: Well, it was a -- I think we spoke a little bit before, you said social -- there was an amount of sociability within the union beside the business aspects of the union. They were very sociable. Musicians were pretty close together, everybody knew practically everybody. And so

98.t: Petrillo and Gray's agreement and why 208 wanted to merge
98.s: They discuss the Petrillo-Gray understanding that kept the locals apart and why Local 208 members voted unanimously to merge: death benefit, taxes and better contracts.
98.q: what this was. That was a real fight. The real fight was preserving the dynasty for the black officials, and then the white officials would -- they didn't want to bring them together.

98.t: Black musicians join Local 10 and win a lawsuit over the fee
98.s: About 200 musicians asked to join Local 10, were charged $45 then $100, sued the International Musicians and won refunds.
98.q: Before this was -- what happened was, a group of the musicians -- we went down to 10 before anything had happened, so far as mergers. It was -- the merger was only talk. So we went down and asked for permission to join 10, about 200 musicians.

98.t: Trusteeship and merger that changed little
98.s: After the International took trusteeship and negotiated with the two unions, the merger left bands as segregated as before.
98.q: Oh, very, very much so. You know why? Because what happened was that after we had done all of this going down and beating our heads against the walls and taking chances and all of that of getting our throats cut and everything, then the International moved in, and then they took trusteeship --

98.t: The Chicago Historical Society concerts and second-class musicians
98.s: DeMichael recalls being unable to hire both locals for 1963 concerts; Saunders says Local 208 members were treated as second class.
98.q: No, no. See, and we couldn't understand how we were paying more taxes and we were paying the same joining fees and whatnot, and we didn't have the same privileges. So it made us like second-class musicians, and we couldn't understand how you could have two locals in one jurisdiction in the same…

98.t: Petrillo as civil rights chairman, and Harry Gray
98.s: Both find it ironic that Petrillo headed the civil rights committee and note Harry Gray opposed integration.
98.q: Civil rights of the Federation, the whole Federation. He was the chairman of the Civil Rights Committee. That was really an insult.

98.t: Missing Local 208 funds, Hal Davis and Saunders's union role
98.s: Only $38,000 and a building were handed over of a reported $250,000; Price Waterhouse could not account for it; Saunders served as assistant to Barney Richards with Leon Washington as business agent.
98.q: No, they couldn't have been, because the way they negotiated, they -- there was a lot of money missing, when they finally were going to merge. They were supposed to have turned over all the assets. They only turned over $38,000 in cash money. And then they had a building, so they turned this…

98.t: Mahalia Jackson's award and the Martin Luther King concert band
98.s: A plaque from Mahalia Jackson honours his 42-piece band for her Martin Luther King concert at the start of union integration.
98.ch: Chicago pioneers, community and New Orleans brotherhood
98.q: Right, well, see this has been my life. I've lived in this neighborhood, this community and things. And a lot of them -- and the awards and things, you know? Now, Mahalia Jackson, there, there's one from Mahalia Jackson up here. And that was given to me in appreciation for a concert that she had…

98.t: Joining the union in 1933 and the 22nd Street boundary
98.s: He joined after the Walkathons; black musicians could not work north of 22nd Street, and business agent Jaborotsky threatened club owners.
98.q: Yeah, right, right. Well, let's see, I think I first started joining the union when I -- in -- when I come to Chicago, here, in 193- -- yeah, about '33.

412.t: First days in New York and the union's restrictions
412.s: Hodes arrives at Bill Kennedy's basement flat with a pregnant wife. He deposits his card at the union and hears all the can'ts and rules for out-of-town men.
412.q: : Well, if you can imagine the -- a couple, just married, two dogs and the Ford full of all our possessions, our few records, just packed, you could barely see out of it. And we're in New York, and there we are. We're in this big town and we find our way way up North there, the…

412.t: Dodging the union delegation and turning down Bunny Berigan
412.s: Hodes sneaks off to the Hickory House past the union delegation and plays nervously. He turns down a job with Bunny Berigan so he can stay and get his card.
412.q: No, he hadn't arrived yet, he hadn't come in. I was -- and Joe hadn't come on the scene yet. Bushkin hadn't arrived. So the next night, I did bring the tuxedo with me, because in Chicago at that time there were so many jobs that called for a tuxedo and you had to own one. The revolution didn't come…

412.t: The New York union's attitude compared with Chicago
412.s: Hodes explains the six-month wait for a card and admires New York's local. He says Chicago's union later told him to ask first, while New York said to go ahead.
412.q: Now, whether that law was right or wrong, I don't know, that they put up that high tariff. And it's not only in New York. I have a great admiration for the local in New York. They're a very -- they see way out, they don't just see the view close up to the eye. Chicago, when I got back to

412.t: The NBC executive and Petrillo's union
412.s: An NBC executive tells Hodes he cannot hire five men when he has 95. Hodes says the union made work for a few.
412.ch: Chicago in the 1950s: Mercury, unions and jobbing
412.q: And so I discovered this about the recording business. But we had all sorts of experiences of going up to the agency and asking me again, what else do you do, we know you play, but what else? I have a friend who's got a vice president of NBC, he's a tremendous friend of him, he owes him a favor.…

412.t: First days in New York and the union's restrictions
412.s: Hodes arrives at Bill Kennedy's basement flat with a pregnant wife. He deposits his card at the union and hears all the can'ts and rules for out-of-town men.
412.q: : Well, if you can imagine the -- a couple, just married, two dogs and the Ford full of all our possessions, our few records, just packed, you could barely see out of it. And we're in New York, and there we are. We're in this big town and we find our way way up North there, the…

412.t: An all-white band at Rupneck's and Chicago's segregated locals
412.s: Hodes ended up with an all-white band at Rupneck's. DeMichael relays Red Saunders's account of the understanding about black bands in the Loop.
412.ch: Return to Chicago: the Blue Note and Rupneck's
412.q: one man. So it didn't work out. Two weeks, I found out I couldn't do a single, there wasn't a jazz joint special. So I came back to Chicago and Skeak came up with a Rupneck's job, and here I am, involved in a jazz band. And again, it turned out to be all white, either Skeak's doing or -- I don't…

122.s: Black musicians had a subsidiary card with no vote, access or committee representation; Curtis Lowe wrote a history.
122.q: Well sure. As a matter of fact I have some documentation that I can get to you. Curtis Lowe who was assistant to our Secretary/Treasurer, they commissioned him to document it, and he wrote a very, very nice documentation. It gives the local number of the first local, the first black local. And then…

122.t: Petrillo abolishes subsidiaries; Local 669 and the 1960 merger
122.s: Local 669 is chartered, a merger is voted down and finally achieved in 1960; he serves on committees and then the Oakland office.
122.q: Our merger. Yeah we merged. Now I drifted once again. I first started out talking about the black local and I told you the story about the merger, and then I joined in ’37 in a Subsidiary. Well as I think I mentioned before, in ’45 or around the mid-forties, Petrillo abolished the subsidiary…

122.t: Union presidents and the abolition of the Oakland office
122.s: After Pop Kennedy, weaker presidents close the Oakland office, membership falls, and he becomes assistant in San Francisco.
122.q: So Pop Kennedy passed away in 1967 then we had another president, kind of a weak president. Kennedy was a strong labor man. He knew all the delegates from our various labor councils and he was on the Executive Board of the American Federation of Musicians. He was a strong labor man. Then when he…

122.t: Effects of the merger: integrated bands but lost representation
122.s: The 49ers band integrates and clubs hire mixed bands, but black musicians lost their officers and convention votes.
122.q: Well yes, on one hand it was positive. The 49er band, they got integrated. Because the 49ers, our football team, they were playing at Keesar Stadium then. That was out in the park. And they had a forty piece band and the band became integrated. And then of course by then, by 1960, many of the clubs…

122.t: Symphony exclusion, redevelopment and the lost Fillmore clubs
122.s: Elaine Jones's treatment, redevelopment wiping out Fillmore clubs, and his own luck with long engagements.
122.q: lady, she had gone to Juilliard, she had played all over Europe, and she played in the symphony, so they wouldn’t let her — the probationary period. So Kurt Adler from the opera orchestra, he took her into the opera orchestra. So she played in the opera orchestra for years. And she went somewhere,…

122.t: Employment restrictions, Barbary Coast history and segregation
122.s: Black bands were shut out east of Divisadero; contrast with the integrated Barbary Coast.
122.q: saying, you had no say and also your employment was restricted. In San Francisco anything east of Divisidero the people wouldn’t hire you. See they wouldn’t hire. The club owners wouldn’t hire, and I told you that story about the Dawn Club and Wilbert Baranco. And now that’s the story that he told…

122.t: Why black musicians were shut out of 1930s jobs
122.s: Puzzling over why twenties jobs closed, he describes union agents blocking work in Oakland and North Beach.
122.q: Well the area was, see we were a minority. The black presence and the Japanese presence, we were very small see. Because you had Russian, French, Irish — the Irish mainly were out in the Mission District, but you had all kind of races here, and Caucasian. And so we were in a very small minority. So…

464.t: Joining the union and the 1959 pension contribution
464.s: He joined the musicians' union through the Newport Youth Band and found his first pension contribution dated 1959.
464.ch: Studio work, Herbie Mann and recording
464.q: I joined the union with the Newport Youth Band, we had to join the union. So, they arranged for us all to go down, and I had practiced all my scales, really worked on my harmonic minor scales.

464.t: The Belafonte cancellation and founding the union's jazz advisory committee
464.s: A cancelled Belafonte date led him to the union, and in 1996 he helped found a jazz advisory committee to sign musicians up for pensions.
464.q: Well, I mean I was a union member, like I said, from 1959. But, I got involved only from the standpoint of probable. I got a call from Harry Belafonte’s office. Harry Belafonte was coming back on the scene. He was going to do a concert at Lincoln Center, or Carnegie Hall, I think it was Carnegie…

464.t: Organizing The New School faculty union and pension
464.s: He helped 75 part-time faculty win union representation with health and AFM pension benefits from 1997.
464.ch: Jazz Master award and teaching career
464.q: Yes. The program started in 1986. By 1996, everybody, there were about 75 part time faculty. We got a check every month. We got taxes taken out, city taxes, state taxes, and federal taxes. We paid social security. I said, “Well, it seems like we’re employees. We are getting all of this stuff taken…

464.t: Why older jazz musicians had no pension
464.s: Musicians bought homes but the pension fund began in 1959, too late for most of them, including Dizzy and Roy Eldridge.
464.q: Yeah, I was not very good friends with Charlie Shavers, I was friends with him. We had played together a couple of times and I had sat in on situations like that. I always respected him and he was fantastic. All these musicians, they made enough money to leave their apartments in Harlem and buy a…

464.t: Gigi Gryce and being blacklisted for speaking up
464.s: They discuss Gigi Gryce, who talked about publishing and rights and was shut out.
464.q: I met Gigi Gryce around Donald Byrd. I want to say that many years later, I played a concert at a school in Queens and Gigi was teaching there. We got to talking at that time. He had his Muslim name. He was a wonderful person; he was tired. He was tired of doing the stuff he had been doing and not…

464.t: Why record companies ignored him; jazz pay and the union
464.s: Owens suspects he lacked a record contract because he spread business information, and they discuss stagnant jazz pay and Local 802.
464.q: Well, I have to say, I get a feeling that a large part of my life is just like that. Record companies didn’t sign me, they signed other trumpet players who could play. I could play also! Maybe I knew too much, I was passing on too much information to too many people. I went many years without a…

83.t: Mixed sessions, the city ordinance and the union
83.s: Interracial sessions risked a city problem and union fines for non-union players; union reps waited outside locked-door sessions.
83.q: Not that it was white union, black union guys playing, but that there'd be non-union guys playing with union guys. Oh, you know, all mixed up. And so it was a double problem, you know. I mean, a lot of, a lot, a lot, a lot of, yeah. Yeah. And it worked both ways. We'd have a mixed band, and it'd be…

83.s: The union forbade overdubbing, then allowed sweetening for film, which record companies used for everything; vocal redubbing was still frowned on but done.
83.q: yeah the union wouldn't allow us to do overdubbing the union decided that you had to hire everybody and do it all at once because they knew obviously it took longer that way so it was a make work kind of thing unions do that sort of thing and the musicians union in particular was in those days very…

83.t: Start of the next tape; the two New Orleans union locals
83.s: The interviewer restarts the tape and asks about unions; Matassa names the two locals, 496 and 174, the Black and white unions.
83.q: Yeah, they should have just added them up and given us the total.

83.t: The Wings session stopped by the union
83.s: Union officials applied rule-book answers rigidly; a session for Wings, a Mercury division, was stopped over the Performance Trust Fund and could only restart after finding the local's president.
83.q: Well, early on, early on, we ran into the problem that the officials of the union, of the unions, were in many ways totally ignorant of the music business, more so than me. And I was pretty dumb about it, okay? And so what they would do is they'd look up the rule book or call the international…

83.t: Union leaders Sidney Cates and Dave Weinstein; inflexible unions
83.s: He remembers the Black local's president Cates and the white local's Weinstein as fine men but inflexible, and thinks the adversarial stance toward record companies was counterproductive.
83.q: Yeah, he was a fine man. I liked him. He was a fine man, but that didn't help anyone that came. It's just like Dave over at the white local. He was a fine guy, you know, real gentleman, nice to speak with.

380.t: Buddy Collette's honors and role in union amalgamation
380.s: Callender and Willard discuss Collette's ACLU awards, his composing, and his work to merge the Black and white locals as one of the first Black studio musicians.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: Mayor Bradley. But we're not talking politics here; only in passing. And the only reason that came up was because Buddy does so many of those kind of gigs, you know. He has I guess you'd say the type of personality that fits in. Buddy is a very gregarious type, and whether he is known to the public…

380.t: Marl Young running for president of Local 47
380.s: They discuss Young's candidacy, his qualifications and history as first Black conductor on a major show.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: Yeah. He's the type of guy that seems to be able to handle everything. I marvel at people like Marl and also our beloved Mayor. I don't see how these people ever rest!

380.t: Two locals did not stop Riddle and McRitchie calling them; You Asked For It
380.s: He was in Local 767 with Collette yet got calls; he describes scoring You Asked For It at ABC to cue.
380.ch: Films, Las Vegas and the union
380.q: I was also a member of 767, just like Buddy. But fortunately, it didn't stop people from calling us to work in pictures, just because there were two locals. They wanted whatever particular talent we had, and a lot of them had nerve enough to call us. Nelson Riddle was another one who didn't let the…

380.t: The Black and White musicians' locals in Los Angeles
380.s: Elmer Fain was business agent; Local 767 was the Black local and 747 the White, with Lester Young's family living beside the Black local.
380.ch: Los Angeles, Ellington and the recording scene
380.q: At that time there were two locals, a Black local and a White local. 767 was the Black local and 747 was the White local. The White local was located on Georgia Street in downtown Los Angeles, and the Black local was on Central Avenue and 18th Street. It's easy to remember, because Lester Young's…

380.t: No residuals for filmed TV shows and the union leadership
380.s: Callender complains that musicians get residuals only on live-audience shows because Petrillo misjudged television.
380.q: No. We only get residuals on the live ones, like Flip Wilson or Carol Burnett, but that's because they were done before a live audience. Other than live audience shows, the band gets nothing. That's one of the beefs we've had. Our leadership is really not on our side in some cases.

8.t: Joining the Chicago musicians' union; the traveling transfer
8.s: Garland resists, then joins the union after the walking delegate pressures the club; he shows a transfer card for the Local 6 move to San Francisco.
8.q: No, no, no, no, no. There wasn't no big girls there, no. Dancing? Dancing and entertaining. Billy Bottoms had the same thing across the way. Then Billy Bottoms, they all got crazy about the jazz band. I could get a job all around. The first time I went to the union, all right, here come the walking…

8.t: Playing the DeLux in Chicago and joining the union
8.s: His band played at the DeLux on 35th and State and was forced into the union by the owner after union pressure.
8.q: I traveled all around. Yeah. And then I come back, you know, and I got a job. Well, we went over in Chicago, such as Blue Monday, Blue Wednesday, Blue Tuesday, the Dreamland and have it on Mondays. DeLux would have it on Tuesdays, T9 Jones, number two, like, different days. And all the entertainers…

8.t: Minor Hall and Baby Dodds swap: Oliver fined by the union
8.s: Oliver dismissed drummer Minor Hall without notice, sent for Baby Dodds without union permission, and the union fined him $200.
8.q: He said, well, uh, he's entitled to notice. He said, notice. He didn't give him his five bucks. I ain't give him nothing.

8.t: Oliver fires Jimmy Palao and the union fines him $200
8.s: Oliver let Jimmy Palao go in San Francisco without notice, Local 6 fined him, and the Plantation date in Chicago was stopped until the fines were paid.
8.q: He played violin. Also clarinet. And Joe let him go. So this boy Minor Hall, we called him Ram, said, 'Well, why are you going to fire this man? We're at the end of the Southern Pacific Line and (Unintelligible). He said, 'I've got a lot to do with it. I don't think it's right.' Then he said,…

635.t: The first musicians' local in New Orleans and John Robichaux
635.s: Foster does not remember the early local, said to date to around 1900; the interviewer mentions Robichaux and dressing neatly.
635.ch: New Orleans bands, players and halls
635.q: That was, that was around, I don't know, 1900, some way back then. Yeah, it would be way back then. See, John, see John, John, John was, wasn't no young man. John was, and he was a fine looking man.

635.t: No union, subbing and a Tuxedo band job anecdote
635.s: Bands were strict, there was no union in the early days, and Foster tells of covering jobs between two bands.
635.ch: Opinions on playing and old New Orleans
635.q: And we had fun. There was no all. See? And we were more strict. The bands were more strict back in them days. And we didn't have no union. We worked with the white union. And we didn't work under no skills. The college didn't have no union. But if you come to hire me, and we'll cut on that price,…

635.t: Unions in New Orleans: none for Black musicians
635.s: He never joined a union in New Orleans; the white musicians had one, and he joined one there around 1925.
635.q: Yeah, but the white, no, no, no, no, no, no union, see. When I went back in 20, in 25 I found a union there that I had to join. But there was no union, see. But the union had a union, because the union there belonged before, but I don't remember they broke up to tell me, but I'd known that about…

635.t: Band uniforms and Noble Sissle; union gold card
635.s: Bands had uniforms with names on the caps, Noble Sissle brought it to New York, and Foster has his Local 802 gold card.
635.q: You see, there's a lot of the guys, see now we, there's something else we used to do down there. Because all the bands down there had their uniforms and their names on the cap of the band. Yeah. See, now that came out of New York, Noble Sissons tried to bring that up in New York, because the band…

157.t: Joining the union at 16 without audition
157.s: Riverside paid his union fees at 16; Monk adds Derek Smith's story of an easy audition.
157.q: Well Riverside, California had a union then and they wanted me to play a show that the Orange County Festival in San Bernardino, the largest city in Riverside at the time, at the county fair. But you had to be union, so they paid for my union fees. I don’t know what it was but I was able to play…

157.t: Union scale for jazz club players
157.s: Hal tried to win club owners' agreements with medical and pension, but many jazz players quit the union.
157.q: Right. I mean most of your good players were in the union. Jazz players were in the union, and then some, like I shouldn’t mention his name but I will because he’s gone now, but John Heard, the great bass player, he was in the union one time and then he quit because the union wasn’t doing anything…

157.t: AFM executive board and running against the AFM president
157.s: Hal explains tensions between large and small locals, Music Performance Trust Fund, and his failed run for AFM president.
157.q: I know it was difficult. And when I was president I was elected to the international executive board and it’s like nine of us at that time telling everybody in the United States and Canada how they’re supposed to work under union contract. And the small locals didn’t like the large locals being…

157.t: How he got involved in Local 47 and became president
157.s: Bob Hardaway got Hal onto the Trial Board; he later ran for vice president and served as president for ten years.
157.q: Yes. When I was a player what got me involved was the president at that time made a deal with the Pantages Theater, a Neiderlander Hotel venue. And so I thought they aren’t helping us. They didn’t give us really an increase in wages or make anything any better. So then a friend of mine, Bob…

0.t: Joining Masonry and the musicians in the lodge
0.s: Caldwell was a mason from 1946; Lem Johnson, the deacon of the blues, and others advanced through the degrees.
0.q: Some do, yeah. Good, now the majority of fellows like Lem Johnson, called the deacon of the blues, and Lem, when I was master, he was my junior warden, but you work around the chairs. You work your way up. And they all join the consistory which you get to 32nd degree in the consistory because…

0.t: Harlem Lodge Number Four masters and musician members
0.s: Caldwell was elected Master in 1949; he lists musician members and later masters such as Eubie Blake, Jonah Jones and Cozy Cole.
0.q: Bob Robinson, tenor saxophone player used to play with fees (unintelligible), Williams and different ones, around New York, and he sponsored me. He was a delegate to the Musicians' Union, Local #802. And Bob was Master, and he

0.t: Does Masonry help musicians' lives? Joppa Lodge and Harlem Lodge
0.s: Caldwell thinks the principles help; Hodges, Carney and Procope belonged to Joppa 55, and he served as a grand lodge officer in the 1960s.
0.q: Johnny belonged to Joppa 55 -- Johnny, Carney, Procop, they joined over there in Joppa 55. They the one that gave Duke, his a masonic funeral too because Duke's mother lodge was in Washington, D. C., but most all these fellows here, they're all living except some that deceased (unintelligible) on…

0.t: Music Dial column and Philadelphia union board
0.s: In Philadelphia he wrote for Music Dial, served two years on the executive board of Local 274, and stays active with his day job and lodge.
0.ch: Later career, civil service and jazz seminars
0.q: Well, I did that -- that happened in '43 to '44, and I came back here, moved back to New York in about November of '44. Then I stayed because I was going over, commuting for being the dean on the executive board of Local #274, elected.

18.s: He joined in March 1929 after a reading test; black and white musicians shared one union, with Petrillo as president.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: Oh, yeah. I was supposed to join in '28 but first then they would test to see if you could read, give you a piece of music and send you across the hall.

18.s: He recalls no musicians' society and says kickbacks ended about 20 years ago.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: No. That left about 20 years ago because, see, you have your scales. If they hire me and the Metropole was open and I go in there, this comes from 802. I have to report to them first and they tell me the scales, how much tax I have to pay each week, and that's what I have to pay. If I don't make…

18.t: Union meetings and Pinky the drummer
18.s: Musicians complained at Local 802 meetings that white players earned more, a fight led by drummer Pinky.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: Yeah, they complained. Sometimes they had meetings. That's why they had meetings down at the Local 802. They brought the scale up and put things even.

18.s: Musicians gave back part of scale; Luis Russell was fined and Otis Johnson refused to kick back.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: They would pay you the scale and you'd give the scale to the union. The union would give you your money and you'd take that $25 or $30 and give it back to the man that owned the place. But they caught up with Louis Russell and put a fine on him. Otis Johnson, trumpet player, said, "I'm not going to…

237.t: Relations with the musicians' union and New York Local 802
237.s: Lovett had no union trouble, and Smith describes the union man waiting in the wings at the Waldorf.
237.q: Yeah, 802. Anyway but we didn't have any trouble. Julia and I went there and we didn't have any trouble at all.

237.t: Hayes's band forced out of Chicago by union rules
237.s: Goodwin explains the Chicago local limited a visiting big band to a few weeks, which hurt them near the Grand Terrace.
237.q: This was Thamon Hayes' and his band, and also later it became Harlan Leonard's band and the Kansas City Rockets. We were in Chicago and we wanted to --

237.t: Traveling musicians, transfers and dues in the locals
237.s: Goodwin and Smith compare transfer rules, ten percent travelling dues and the cost of joining Local 34627.

237.t: Union fines for working under scale end Hayes's career
237.s: Ramsey reported them to the union; each man was fined $50 and Hayes $500, which took him out of music and left Harlan Leonard the band.
237.q: I don't know. He was foreign to us, he was from Chicago and we were Kansas City -- most of us were from Kansas City people

171.t: McShann out of the Army, Ben Webster and Tiny Grimes
171.s: Barry Ulanov pressed him to return to McShann but Ramey explained the union rule, then worked with Ben Webster and Tiny Grimes.
171.ch: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
171.q: through. Now McShann gets out of the Army. Naturally, and I've got to go six months before I can work with out of town musicians. So Barry Ulanov and several of them come over there almost threatening me, you know, said, 'Look, you got to go back with McShann. He needs you, and you need him because…

171.t: McShann's seven-piece opening group and the local's zoning objection
171.s: Seven pieces opened including Bob Mabane, a baritone and singer Joe Williams; the white local claimed they were out of territory.
171.ch: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
171.q: No, they had this alto player, some a tall old boy that played in Bus Moten Mosley's band. And we just got through calling his name the other day. Had a trumpet player, Anderson, I think his name was.

171.t: Settling in New York: Lips Page and the Local 802 probation
171.s: Lips Page got him work on 52nd Street while the union barred him from out-of-town bands for six months.
171.ch: New York: 52nd Street and Lester Young
171.q: Well, I -- first of all, I got into Lips -- saw Lips, and he told me, said, 'Why don't you stay in town?' I said, 'Well, I want to, but I can't get nothing down on 52nd Street.' He said, 'Well, that's a clique,' but he said, 'I'll get you in two nights a week with me.'

171.t: Playing with Bus Moten's group and the union threat
171.s: After the walkathon he worked briefly with Bus Moten's group and was threatened by the union to join in 1934.
171.q: Yeah, Benny Moten died, and see, these guys were trying to get that Reno club after Basie left, see. By this time Basie had gone to New York, you know. In fact, he'd been gone for some time. But anyway, it was in '36 or '37.

79.t: Charlie Turner's Arcadians, and the union pulling him off
79.s: Thomas worked with Charlie Turner's Arcadians at the Arcadia Ballroom, with Bobby Stark and Emmett Matthews, until the New York union pulled him off for lacking a card.
79.q: See, in those days you've got to get around so people know you're in town. So a fellow by name of Charlie Turner, a fat man had a group (something about around the world) ...

79.t: How he got to Fletcher Henderson's house
79.s: Turner told Thomas he'd soon be with Fletcher Henderson, and the union could scare you. Through Keg Johnson, Thomas rehearsed at Henderson's house.
79.q: Because he looks like he could fight instead of play the trumpet ... Charlie always said when we got together, he has a place at 155th street, yeah, Fletcher Henderson, get away from me. Well, in those days here's a guy and I'm sure he's the best now. I'm sure he wouldn't mind it and the unions had…

79.t: Joe Jordan and the union agent Peek-a-boo Jimmy
79.s: Thomas explains the union agent Peek-a-boo Jimmy, who tried to stop out-of-town musicians from working in New York, and starts to describe Joe Jordan.
79.q: Ferman Tapps, yes. Well, a fellow by the name of Joe Jordan, he passed about a couple years ago. He was about 80 or 90 years old.

79.t: Joe Jordan gets him into Ferman Tapp's band and the union
79.s: Sick with a stomach problem and wanting a New York card, Thomas left Henderson. Jordan sent him to banjoist Ferman Tapp, which got him into the union; he worked there three months.
79.q: Yeah and I wanted to get the New York card, you know. So, Joe Jordan, whom I have tremendous respect for, I didn't know him before. I knew his name and I'm sure he didn't know me and we did some things at ... later on, ... respect for him. So one night he talks to me, he says, You Joe Thomas? I…

121.t: Joining the union and the black local 496's books
121.s: Ridgley's in-and-out union membership since 1949, bought cards, double books at the black local.
121.q: Well I've been, I've been in and out the union since 1949. Like the way you said that in and out. Yeah. Well I was, I, you know I would be in and then I would drop out and then I would get back in and drop out. Well I've been in this stretch, this stretch I've been in since 19, I think since 1960.…

121.t: Union checks, money and the board
121.s: Ridgley on right to work, a quarter million dollars through the union, and being threatened with the board.
121.q: Yeah, they would check, you know. And more hassle, you know, than anything. That right to work wasn't so much enforced then like it is now. Because the union don't even bother you no more. They leave it up to you to take care. See like last Friday night I played at the Royal Lawley bourbon all the…

121.t: Ridgley's view of the union and recording-session delegates
121.s: He thinks unions have outlived usefulness; Tad recalls delegates sitting in on sessions, and Mr. Green stopping recordings.
121.q: 496, well, they had me before the boat every other week. Well, for failing to file a contract. I didn't do this yet. You know, and I thought there was a bunch of dogs. In fact, the union as a whole, I think, you know, people, a lot of people get on me when I say this because there are people who…

681.t: His father's spot jobs and the musicians' union building on Bourbon Street
681.s: His father played trumpet taps at Italian society events, was vice president of Local 174 and engineered the cheap Depression purchase of the union home; a larger Elks building was turned down.
681.q: Uh-huh. And, uh... The... And then, uh... He did play music... On the side. He played some spot jobs, you may... Would say. Uh... One... One thing I do remember... That he was... There was a couple of organizations... Fraternal organizations... Primarily Italian organizations... That, uh... They…

681.t: Union home plaque and Jacques Pepitone's WWL speech
681.s: Hirsch recalls the union home and a missing plaque, then tells of union president Pepitone's gaffe at the WWL 50,000-watt dedication.
681.q: That was over in Mandeville. And, I had to go to a meeting one day and I was supposed to take my wife to the racetrack, which I didn't take. And I went to the meeting and she went down there and she says, well, for missing the racetrack, there's one thing that I wanted. Because we had sold at home…

681.t: Charlie Wagner stories and losing old friends
681.s: Wagner's Jean Lafitte Rose publicity stunt, his Lafitte job with no union, and Hirsch's sadness at losing Ray Bonitas and other friends.
681.q: I still got the picture of it. So we go up to somewhere, by the school, by the library up there. And we get a little girl and dress her up in like a little pirate's costume with a bandana around her head like this. And we're both standing there. And I got a shovel, and Charlie's there pointing at…

303.t: Praise for the union president Dave
303.s: Allen and Riddick talk about Dave's cooperation with the interviews, his lost election to an international union post, and his honesty.
303.q: Dave is one of the finest men, you know. He lost the election on an international board member, vice president of the international union. He lost that.

303.t: Unqualified players and the musicians' union
303.s: Riddick objects to the union admitting bass players and band leaders who fake playing and take jobs from real musicians; Allen recalls Johnny Wiggs criticizing a hotel band.
303.q: Yeah, well, he... But I don't know how much. He never was a good bass player because he never, he didn't do anything but pick it up and start fooling with it and think he could play. That's the way plenty of them are today. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Yeah. They got bass players today that don't even know how to…

303.t: Black intermission quartet and union integration
303.s: Black musicians' intermission group at the Famous Door, when bands integrated and the unions merged.
303.q: Oh yes. Oh yes. We played guitar and alto sax. Teddy Purnell played alto. Smiley and Joe played guitar. Alton Purnell played piano. Alonzo Duke Stewart played drums. They were all black men. See, we weren't at that time playing together in mixed colors.

199.s: Union officials stopped the music at the Dew Drop and everyone had to join the union in December 1952.
199.q: You got to be in a union, man. And everybody in there, nobody had... No one had a card. So we all had to go down the next day and go apply for the card. 1952. I'll never forget that. December, 1952. So then we went down and joined the union. That's what happened.

199.t: The union merger and why members left
199.s: Cotton recalls vague conflict over merging Black and white locals and says the union does little, while his government pension makes him independent.
199.q: Oh, when they were trying to decide whether they were going to merge. It was some kind of conflict. I don't know what it was. I really wasn't concerned about it because I think I was going in and out of town at the time. So it really didn't concern me too much.

199.t: Club owners and the union's weakness today
199.s: Clubs in the Quarter are run by Italian owners and managers, union scale is rarely paid, and higher scale cost bands a front-line player.
199.q: I mean, you know, Italian people usually run things down there. You know, I don't know who, I don't say they're the mafia, but the people who were running things, you know. Several of them have died out. The place where I was, at least two or three of them have died, you know.

101.t: The union dues Basie owed the band
101.s: Terry gets the union secretary to force Basie to repay $357 to each member.
101.q: This was – I think we used to pay 1% – 3% tax – work dues, they called them – of which we were returned 1%. It had gone on for a long period of time. At this point each member of the band was due back about $357. I kept abreast of it. I kept saying, said, “[?], we’re going – you’re going to have to…

101.t: Break and resumption of the second session
101.s: The recording stops and Brower resumes with Basie economics.
101.q: Did it get dark a little? My eyes are always playing tricks on me. I’m gonna go get me another toothpick.

101.t: Union trouble and scab gigs on Olive Street
101.s: Terry could not get a union card and worked cheaper non-union joints, once with Betty Roche and Jimmy Forrest.
101.q: The union was – they were more society than anything else. I stayed around there. I played scab gigs. I couldn’t get in the union. They wouldn’t give me a union gig. I couldn’t get a union card. So I used to go down to Olive Street. They had three or four little joints down there where they paid…

400.t: Chicago's black union local, its merger with the white local
400.s: Hinton explains the black local's wealth from touring bands, the white local president's claim to downtown, and his ending of separate unions in the federation.
400.ch: Capone's Chicago, the union and hired by Cab
400.q: Well it was special and it was progressive in the west end but they destroyed themselves. At first all of the clubs and things and the work was on the south side so there wasn‟t that much work downtown, so the white union wanted to join. [Unintelligible] said no because all of the bands that came…

400.t: The Cotton Club opening and the Local 802 card crisis
400.s: Hinton had only a Chicago union card at the 1936 Cotton Club dress rehearsal; Claude Jones and Keg Johnson talked Cab into keeping him.
400.ch: Cotton Club, Zutty and Chicago traditions
400.q: Yeah. I stayed in his band 16 years. We opened the Cotton Club in 1936, opened the Cotton Club at 48th and Broadway. Big show, we rehearsed it. [Laugh] I got no union… I got no 802 union card. I‟ve got the Chicago card. The dress rehearsal night [laugh] the union comes in to see everybody‟s card…

400.t: The musicians' trust fund and the Carnegie Hall benefit loan fund
400.s: Hinton learns a federation fund exists for destitute musicians, and explains the benefit concerts that created a fund he and Mona help run, lending up to $500.
400.ch: Capone's Chicago, the union and hired by Cab
400.q: That‟s right. That‟s really true. And also, most people don‟t know, there is a mature fund, a very huge fund in the American Federation of Musician, a trust fund for any musician that becomes destitute and most people that we know that have problems don‟t know that you can go to that.

80.t: Auditioning for Charlie Johnson; Kenneth Roane; Local 802 card
80.s: Kenneth Roane vouched for him to Charlie Johnson, and Mr. Small had him taken to Local 802 for a union card.
80.ch: New York, Henderson and Charlie Johnson
80.q: Charlie Johnson, yeah. So little things like that, picked up a couple of dollars, kept me eating. So I went down to Charlie Johnson's, and I had met Ham Davis, who's a trumpet player. I had met Charlie. Oh, drummer, uh, I'll recall his name in a minute. One of the greatest guys -- uh, I -- oh,…

80.t: Marches from school, and playing 'Poet and Peasant' for his union card
80.s: He still remembers a dozen Sousa marches and overtures, and at his Local 802 audition in 1933 an official said he could jazz the Poet and Peasant overture.
80.q: Yeah. Now for instance, I can play -- I am pretty sure -- I haven't done it in a long time, but about a dozen standard marches I memorized back in my school days.

80.t: Complaints about the Local 802 musicians' union and no pension
80.s: The union offers him no pension, only a senior membership card worth nothing, and he says it ignores musicians; he relies on Social Security, and Rudy Powell once worked there before his stroke.
80.q: No. From the union they wish you would drop dead soon, because they don't want to pay you that thousand -- that's all they're going to give you, the thousand dollars, anyway. And they wouldn't give a damn. I mean you could fall dead, and jump out a window, and who cares. This came the other day.

230.t: Glen Island Casino: the all-New York band and interference
230.s: To meet union rules he had to replace out-of-town musicians for the Glen Island Casino, where management dictated repertoire and compared him to Casa Loma.
230.ch: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
230.q: Well, again Milton Romer to the front. He worked out of -- I guess he didn't give up on me. He got me the job at the Glen Island Casino. Now, I had this band that I'd been rehearsing, and you know, doing some work around, a little work around with it, and it was a travelling band, and by that, they…

230.t: Love and Hisses and sideline musicians in films
230.s: His acting in Love and Hisses was only waving a baton while a record played; union rules required real musicians on camera, and Los Angeles had separate Black and white locals.
230.q: No, they were playing a record back. It had been recorded. Everybody that was in the picture was -- not one of them was on the record. Sideline, they call that.

230.t: Union membership and weak union scale
230.s: He was not in the union as Fred Black; the union was weak and studio pay was about 20 dollars for as many sides as possible.
230.q: The union was terribly weak at that time, anyway. It wasn't really much chance of getting in much trouble, because there wasn't anybody in town that was getting paid union scale, except maybe some studio musicians, and even that the rates were so low, like you'd go into a recording studio and for…

677.t: Joining the Musicians Union and Local 767
677.s: He joined in late 1927 when the Black local 767 met in a garage, with few benefits and little enforcement compared with white Local 47.
677.q: '27, yes, I joined the Musician's Union in the latter part of 1927, and it was very new at that time. In fact, our union office was in the garage of one of the fellows, back in the alley there off of Central Avenue.

677.t: Why he joined the union and its gold card
677.s: He joined because the union was gaining power, and later received a gold card for thirty years' membership.
677.q: Well, it became imperative. The union was getting power. And you joined the union, you're way ahead you know. You're eventually going to do it anyway, so you might as well be ahead.

677.t: Mr. Robinson, the garage owner behind Local 767
677.s: The older mechanic whose garage housed the union acted as secretary.
677.q: I said, they didn't have money enough to hire a hall or have a place of their own, so this old man was just good enough to allow them to use the back room of his garage.

120.t: The Omer Hicks band, Roseland, and the Ross Gorman job the union blocked
120.s: Chubb-Steinberg becomes the Omer Hicks band and tours East; at Roseland he meets Red Nichols and Miff Mole and is offered Gorman's chair but cannot join the New York union.
120.ch: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
120.q: Well, sure because he had some work going through at that time an agent, I think, and, uh, he put on a different saxophone player-on the tenor, there was a guy named P.T.---

120.t: Rumors, Petrillo, and losing his union card
120.s: The drunk rumor spreads and Petrillo, using a wrongly signed contract at a Black ballroom as pretext, pulls his card, later returning it.
120.q: : And, a lot of people actually thought that. You know, they really thought that and that was a very bad time for me. At the union, at that time, even Petrilla, who was trying --- he even made the crack at one time that he was going to get me one way or the other---

120.t: Moving to Chicago, union rules, and the Benson Office jackets
120.s: Chicago's union makes him work one-nighters for six months; the Benson booking office sends him out with rotating coloured jackets.
120.ch: Chicago, Detroit and Seattle Harmony Kings
120.q: Yeah, I went back to Defiance and, of course, uh, I had a taste of Cincinnati and I also got a look at Chicago and I wanted to go to Chicago. And, I think I went back to Cincinnati just to see Carl and the guys, from my home town. And, I was determined --- I was just determined that I wanted to --…

235.t: New York's six-month grace period and strict union enforcement
235.s: He explains the six-month wait for a union card in New York, strict delegates who pulled people off jobs, and that Detroit's union had been more relaxed.
235.ch: The Paradise and life in Queens

406.ch: Zach White, Cotton Pickers and Cab Calloway
406.q: Now, the union grabbed Cab for bringing me into New York. I wasn't a member of the union. Brought him in. In between theaters and Cotton Club we had to go to the union meetings before the trial board. This went on for a couple of weeks. And he was driving back and forth. And finally they decided to…

1.t: Getting paid by Luckey Roberts: the union hearing and the wrong address
1.s: Danny had to take Roberts to the union to be paid after six months, and Roberts gave wrong addresses because he kept three women.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: If you worked with Luckey Roberts, you never got your money til later. I played a gig with him, it was six months; I had to bring him to the union to get paid. When I get to the union, he's there, and he's been ...(?)... it all before (?) like that. And he's there, and you go before the board for a…

145.t: Merging the black and white musicians' unions
145.s: Royal discusses the long fight to merge Local 767 into Local 47, officers, his father's union presidency and why 47 needed the money.
145.ch: Billie Holiday, Basie leadership and studio work
145.q: That was when he got involved, because Buddy was just a young man at that time. He was in his early 20s and there had been other fellows that had worked out there

88.t: Union forces Lester to play from the floor as a guest
88.s: Because of the separate locals, Lester had to wait on a milk box and play three tunes in each set from the floor for six weeks while his transfer went through.
88.ch: Hampton, New York and Lee's own band
88.q: And so -- as I stated before, they thought that I was gonna axe Bumps and have Lester in the band, but I intended to have both of them in the band.

27.t: Willis Young's playing, last meeting in 1930 and later union job
27.s: Phillips says Willis Young could not play as well as Lester but praised Phillips's power; he last saw him in Montana in 1930, and Young later held an important union post in Los Angeles and died in 1943.
27.q: : Oh, no! Hell, no. Shit, he couldn't gooder than me! That's why he liked me so well. He said, "You blow just like Joe Oliver and Louis Armstrong" -- I'd never met them, you know. He said, "You got a lot of power." He said, "They have power. Now, if you was in New Orleans on one of them parades,…

68.t: Leaving Basie in 1950; Lucky Millinder and the Local 802 transfer rule
68.s: Tate, waiting out the three-month union rule, is put to work by Millinder.
68.q: I was in the union and I see Lucky Millinder in the union, Local 802, it was on Sixth Avenue then, so he said, "What's going on over there?" So I says, "Well, the band's breaking up." He says, "That's what I heard." He says, "What are you going to do?" I said, "I can't do anything." I says, "I got…

409.t: Union card problem keeps him from working with Chick
409.s: As a Mobile union member with no New York card he was barred from working with Chick Webb, though free to work with others.
409.q: about music. Of course, I didn't stay with him very long. I didn't stay with Chick very long. I'll tell you what happened. See, I had my Mobile card. I didn't have a New York 802 card.

378.t: Waiting for a New York union card; society band work
378.s: Barred from the Biltmore job by union rules, he freelances with Meyer Davis and Lanin, as all the stars did.
378.ch: New York bands and the first records
378.q: Year. Not Six months like right now. Had to take a year, they were trying to keep people out. Everyone wanted to come to New York then.

166.t: Warwick Hall and the segregated Chicago unions
166.s: On Thursday nights the Musicians' Union held jam nights with Locals 208 and 10 and meager shares.
166.ch: Records, Blanton, the Chicago scene, Nat Cole and Nadine
166.q: Well, this was around early '37 that I played with King Kolax out here. But then I ran into him in Chicago, and they had a hall there, the Warwick Hall. Where all musicians graduated from, like Gene Ammons graduated from there with King Kolax.

231.t: Tape change and the unions and guilds a performer must join
231.s: Side B of Tape 12; he lists AGVA, AFTRA, SAG, Negro Actors Guild and Equity as required for welfare benefits.
231.ch: Television, the stroke and later reflections
231.q: You'd be surprised how many different organizations you have to belong to to get in this business and be on the ground floor. Do you know that? You've got to belong to AGVA, AFTRA, SAG, NAG and Equity. American Guild of Variety Artists, American Federation for Theater and Radio, Negro Actors Guild,…

89.t: Black musicians and the white union local in 1920
89.s: Black musicians were not in the white local, freelanced without protection, and 802 was formed once they became competition.
89.q: No, no. As a matter of fact, in New York then there was no such -- 802 was just young and 21 -- in 1920 there wasn't any 802, there was 308 or 310 or something like that.

28.t: Freddie's sneaky pete, a union man and the envied suits
28.s: Freddie hid a gallon of cheap wine behind his drums, and a union delegate named Huey forced Butler to join the local, while Freddie wanted suits like Butler's.
28.q: He said, but you don't understand, man, I said in Canada yes, Freddie -- now, we have/ -- they got all the nice whiskey that they make, they got some of the best beer in the world, and that Russian Black Horse, they got them all, Freddie had a big gallon of sneaky pete behind his drums. And loved…

381.t: How his father paid for his Local 802 union membership
381.s: Facing a union threat at the Rosebud, his father arranged a night shift on the WPA and claimed sick pay to raise the $54.
381.q: I'm gonna tell you a funny story. After working at the Rosebud for about 3 weeks, the union representative -- I don't know if you remember him -- Redman.

758.s: Playing at the Palace Theatre with Mal Hallett, who agreed to pay scale to protect him from Glaser's cut.
758.ch: Glaser, the Arcadia and bands of 1939-41
758.q: : So what happened was that... Heh-heh. I went on my tour. I was going up to play for Scribner(?). He's the one who used to book all the bands in New England. And I played a date with Mal Hallett's band.

147.t: The 802 union keeps Lunceford's band out; Peekaboo Davis
147.s: Crawford says Local 802 refused them membership to slow the band, a delegate named Peekaboo Davis policed it, and they used Buffalo's local 533.
147.ch: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
147.q: -- by chance -- no, they wouldn't let us in the union. By no means. They were trying to break the band up. We were going -- we were growing too fast.

453.t: Union trouble as a transfer member from Milwaukee
453.s: The Chicago local blocked him from a Regal Theater job as a transfer member, but could not remove him from Louis Armstrong's band because Armstrong insisted.
453.q: No, because I guess I was busy trying to weather the storm of my own thing by being transfer member from Milwaukee in here, and it looked like this union had it in for transfer members, because I was to go into Regal Theater with Jerome Carrington and I think George Smith was president

383.t: Trained as a printer but shut out by segregated unions
383.s: Wilson graduated Tuskegee in 1928 as a printer but could not get Detroit newspaper work because the printers' union was white only; he lists segregated musicians' locals.
383.q: But there was one serious flaw. Now, for instance, in my own case, I came out of Tuskegee, I graduated high school there in 1928. And with excellent -- as a printer.

93.s: Chuckles learned the vibraphone and they were made honorary musicians' union members; Green compares dancers on xylophone and vibraphone.
93.q: Well, we introduced new songs and new tap dances and so on. And Chuckles eventually learned how to play a musical instrument, which was the vibraphone. And we had become honorary musicians by being with Buck and Bubbles. They made us members of the musicians' union. And most of the unions at that…

99.t: Palais Royale in Buffalo and the union frame-up
99.s: The band is barred from working for two years after union officials trick them into playing below scale at Buffalo's Palais Royale.
99.q: back in those times, $50.00 a week. We worked on that job the whole -- the rest of the summer. '29. // -- and they booked us into the Palais Royale in Buffalo, New York, to open in September, 1929. Beautiful nightclub, we had to play a luncheon engagement, we had to play a dinner engagement, we'd…

611.t: Philadelphia's two unions and joining local 802 in New York
611.s: Waters joined the Black local in Philadelphia at about 16 and only joined New York's local 802 around 1926, when he came with Charlie Johnson from Atlantic City.
611.ch: Other Philadelphia work and the union
611.q: soon as they joined, going uptown, they joined the, this uptown on 133rd Street. The Symphony Club or somethin' like that.

169.t: Rochester trio, first Social Security card, joining the union
169.s: He takes a trio job in Rochester, Minnesota, gets his first Social Security card, and returns to St. Paul where he has to join the union.
169.q: So I had to cut out from that band. I went with a trio down to Rochester, Minnesota, where the Mayo Clinic is. We went down there, and that's when they brought in Social Security... I guess I went around '36 or '37, or '38 maybe. The guy started collecting Social Security. So we didn't understand…

19.t: Deciding to be a professional musician; joining the union in 1938
19.s: After the Miles band he never again holds another kind of job.
19.ch: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
19.q: me into the professional thing. That was finally when I really decided that I'm not going to do anything else; you're doing this and... I would go from one job to another, and I never had another job doing anything else since I was a kid. I sold newspapers, but since I'd started playing the piano…

115.t: Black union local 627 and who could sit in
115.s: Gus explains the Black local 627 in Kansas City, its president Shaw and how a ten-cent beer bought a blind eye to sitting in.
115.ch: Kansas City, Omaha and Lloyd Hunter
115.q: And I couldn't sit in and play, no way. The president of the union would come by and he wouldn't want you to sit in and play with anybody, unless you joined the union.

31.t: Ethel Waters at the Lafayette, Earl Dancer and the union
31.s: He made orchestrations for Ethel Waters, producer Earl Dancer ran off with the money, and Whaley took the manager to the union and was kept out of the theatre for a year.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: I didn't run into Claude until after -- Claude was playing down at the Roseland, and this was in '28, and I got the job at the theatre, see, and I got a band and went into the Lafayette Theatre.

389.t: Non-union bands, failing the union test and getting in
389.s: Early local bands had no bottom; he flunked his union reading test, then got in when pianist Freddie Small vouched for him.
389.q: That's right. Non-union jobs. We played with a fiddle player. The usual band at that time was a fiddle, MR. GITLER: MR. CHALLIS: a saxophone, no bottom --^N accordinos, ?^N no accordions. Piano, banjo, and drums. Between the drums and the banjo that's where your rhythm came from but there was…

75.t: Erroll Garner at Tondelayo's and joining Local 802
75.s: Ramirez admired Erroll Garner's chords, introduced him in Willie Bryant days, and helped him join the union after Bill Bailey objected.
75.ch: The war years: Barnet, Hot Lips Page, Newton and Kirby
75.q: As I said before, we were working that night at Tondelayo's(?), and Erroll... Erroll was so magnificent a player. I mean, I never saw anybody handle chords on the keyboard like him at that time. The more he played, the more he liked to play, and the fact that I was listening to him made him go on…

77.t: Townsend's later success as Redcaps president
77.s: He wrote her during Show Boat thanking her, became president of the Redcaps and CIO board member, and they stayed platonic friends until he died.
77.ch: Records, Lovie Austin and a first marriage
77.q: -- in London, yes -- I received a letter from him saying he just didn't -- a note to the woman who had won. He didn't want to prove on my success and all, but just a note to the woman who had won, because he had gone to school in Canada and got a degree in commercial --

455.t: Unionizing the Moonglow job in Baltimore with Roy Eldridge
455.s: Budd and Roy Eldridge jam at a non-union club, and Budd gets his union card paid and takes over the job as leader.
455.ch: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
455.q: Well, Cubie was -- Cubie was -- was fronting the band. So, me and Roy used to get together and talk, so we used to go down to a place called the Moonglow. And, Ruben Blakely was the emcee there.

529.t: Union 802 hiring floor and prejudice in music
529.s: Sam says only white names are called for gigs on the union floor and that prejudice exists everywhere.
529.q: And all you can hear is Weinstein. You can't hear no Mitchells and Jones and Smiths and Johnsons. They don't have none of them.

13.t: Being the youngest in the band, and the union in the twenties
13.s: He was usually the youngest man in older bands and got work by recommendation rather than through the union.
13.q: Well, it's hard to say, because as I remember back in the twenties, like I was -- in most bands I was in, I was the youngest man in the band. It's not like it is nowadays with these rock bands, where you all start out together.
